core.text: After a comparative you can drop *quam* (than) and put the thing compared in the ablative: **the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he)**. *Canis lupō ferōcior est* — the dog is fiercer than a wolf; *nihil melle dulcius est* — nothing is sweeter than honey. The ablative usually stands right before the comparative. Latin name: *ablātīvus comparātiōnis*.
*Than* in English introduces the second half of a comparison: *braver than he*. Latin can leave the word out and let the case say it.
Comparative + ablative = 'than …'. With quam the two things are in the same case: *canis ferōcior est quam lupus*.

Two ablatives can sit around one comparative: *multō māior frātre* — bigger than his brother by much. The person is the ablative of comparison; **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multo maior = bigger by much)** is the measure (*multō, paulō, nihilō*).

more.text: The learner's notes (week 24) give *hic illō fortior est*, *haec illīs meliōra sunt*, *nihil hōc peius esse potest*. Ørberg glosses it in cap. XXIV: *melior frātre meō = melior quam frāter meus*; *stultior vōbīs = stultior quam vōs*.

The ablative is used only when the first thing compared is nominative or accusative; otherwise Latin keeps *quam*. It is the normal choice after negatives and in set phrases: *lūce clārius* (clearer than daylight), *opīniōne celerius* (faster than expected), *plūs aequō* (more than fair). Comparative adverbs take it too: *ventō celerius* — faster than the wind.

teach.title: The word for 'than' can disappear
teach.say: After a comparative, Latin may drop *quam* (than) and put the thing compared into the ablative instead: **the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illō fortior = braver than he)**. *Mārcus Quīntō māior est* — Marcus is bigger than Quintus. Nothing has gone missing; the case is doing the work of the word.

teach.title: Where it stands, and what it looks like
teach.say: It nearly always sits immediately before its comparative, and it wears the plain ablative ending of its own declension: *lupō*, *aquā*, *illō*, *hostibus*. There is no preposition in front of it, and that bare ablative is the tell: *Canis lupō minor est*.

show.say: lupō — the bare ablative, with no preposition in front of it

teach.title: Pronouns do it too
teach.say: The same ablative serves for *mē*, *tē*, *hōc*, *illō*, *eō*: *Frāter meus mē prūdentior est* — my brother is wiser than I am. After a negative word it is the usual way to say it: *Nihil hōc pēius esse potest*, nothing can be worse than this.

teach.title: Two ablatives round one comparative
teach.say: *Iūlius multō māior est frātre suō.* Two ablatives, two different jobs: *frātre* is the person compared, and *multō* is **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multō māior = bigger by much)** — by how much bigger. The measure words are few and worth knowing by sight, *multō* and *paulō*, and each stands immediately in front of its own comparative.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: It works with any comparative, singular or plural, adjective or adverb: *Mīlitēs Rōmānī hostibus fortiōrēs erant*. Turn it into English with 'than'. When the first thing compared is neither the subject nor the object, Latin keeps *quam* and puts both halves in the same case instead.
